title: Thinking Before Starting
keyIdea: Before you start something new, stop and think: what do I already know about this? You nearly always know something. Waking it up gives the new ideas a place to stick, and it helps you spot what you wonder about. A short think before you start saves wrong tries. Stop, think, wonder, then start.

kid: Something new is coming. Stop for a moment. Ask: what do I know about this?
You know more than you think. Before a lesson on bees, you may know that bees buzz. You may have seen one on a flower. Those are things you know.
Now ask: what do I wonder? How do bees make honey? That is a question to find out. Things you know tell. Things you wonder ask.
Then start. A short think first helps you make fewer mistakes. But do not think for ages. Think a bit, then go.
adult: This is a metacognition habit: activating prior knowledge before a task. The EEF guidance on metacognition and self-regulated learning puts it in the planning stage (what do I already know that will help?), before monitoring and evaluating. The EYFS characteristics of effective learning call the same move making links and planning, and it carries into Key Stage 1 when children start new topics and simple investigations.

The idea goes back to Ausubel: the most important single thing for learning is what the learner already knows. New facts are easier to remember when they join up with old ones, which psychologists call a schema. Donna Ogle's KWL chart (Know, Want to know, Learned) makes the habit visible. Children list what they know, write what they wonder, and come back at the end to add what they learned.

Common mistakes: saying 'I know nothing' about a new topic, when a little prompting shows they do; rushing straight in and repeating wrong tries; mixing up a fact with a question in a KWL chart; and linking to things that are true but not related (my bike is red). Be careful not to make the think so long that it becomes waiting. A short pause of a few seconds to a minute is enough at this age.

In the lab your child drags bee facts into a think cloud (and leaves out facts that are not about bees), sorts Know and Wonder cards, races Rush against Sam with a think time they choose, picks the thing they already know that helps with a new job, and puts Stop, Think, Wonder and Start in order. Every drag has a button twin.

familyTip: Before a new book, trip or game, ask 'What do we already know about this?' and say two things each. Then ask 'What do we wonder?' Afterwards, check: did we find out?

visual.caption: Is it something you know, or something you wonder? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: The moon is in the sky at night.
Why does the moon change shape?

lab.caption: Flagship lab: wake up what you know, sort Know and Wonder cards, race with a think time you choose, use what you know, and put your think plan in order.

practice.prompt: Thinking before starting: you are about to learn about snails. What do you do first?
choices: Think: what do I already know about snails?
Start as fast as I can
Say I know nothing about snails
practice.hint: Before you start, stop. What could you already know about snails?
practice.explain: Thinking first wakes up what you know, like snails have shells. New snail facts then have a place to stick.

practice.prompt: Rush starts a puzzle at once and makes {n} wrong tries. Sam stops to think first and makes 0 wrong tries. How many more wrong tries did Rush make?
practice.hint: Take Sam's wrong tries away from Rush's: {n} take away 0.
practice.explain: {n} take away 0 is {n}. Rush made {n} more wrong tries because he did not stop to think.

practice.prompt: Which card goes under I wonder?
practice.hint: I wonder cards ask something you want to find out. Look for a question.
practice.explain: What do snails eat? asks a question, so it goes under I wonder. The other two tell things you know.

practice.prompt: You think of {n} things you know about bees. Then you think of 2 more. How many things do you know now?
practice.explain: {n} and 2 more make {=n+2}. The more you wake up, the more links new facts can join.

pool.prompt: You are about to make a paper plane. Which thing you know will help?
choices: I can fold paper in half
pool.hint: Which one is about paper and folding?
pool.explain: Folding paper in half links to making a paper plane. The others are true, but they do not help with this job.

pool.prompt: Leo stops and thinks for a short time before a new game. What happens?
pool.hint: In the race, what happened when Sam looked first?
pool.explain: A short think helps you plan, so you make fewer wrong tries. Sam finished first after a short look.

pool.prompt: Which card goes under I know?
pool.hint: I know cards tell a thing. They do not ask.
pool.explain: Rain is wet tells a fact, so it goes under I know. The other two are questions to wonder about.

pool.hint: You stop first, and you start last.
pool.explain: Stop, think what you know, wonder what to find out, then start.

pool.prompt: Sam looks at the puzzle box for {n} seconds, then takes 6 seconds to build it. How many seconds is that in all?
pool.hint: Add the looking time and the building time: {n} and 6.
pool.explain: {n} seconds of looking and 6 seconds of building make {=n+6} seconds.

pool.prompt: Ava says, 'I know nothing about the sea.' But she has been to the beach. What is true?
choices: She knows some things, like the sea is salty
She should not think about it
pool.hint: Think about what she saw and felt at the beach.
pool.explain: Ava knows things from the beach, like waves and salty water. Stopping to think wakes them up.

pool.prompt: A KWL chart has {n} I know cards and 3 I wonder cards. How many cards is that?
pool.hint: Count the I know cards, then count on 3.
pool.explain: {n} I know cards and 3 I wonder cards make {=n+3} cards.

pool.prompt: Should you think for a very, very long time before you start?
choices: No, a short think is enough
pool.hint: In the race, was the longest look the fastest?
pool.explain: A short think helps. Thinking for a very long time is just waiting, so think a bit and then start.
